title.en: Mula Jadi Na Bolon: The Batak Creation and the Naga Padoha Beneath
title.zh: 穆拉·賈迪·納·波隆：巴塔克創世與地下那伽

region.en: Toba Batak country and Mount Pusuk Buhit, North Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘多巴巴塔克之地與普素·布希山

texts.period: Batak cosmogonic tradition recorded by H. N. van der Tuuk (J.R.A.S., N.S. vol. XIII, 1860s) and later ethnography

source.work: Batak cosmogonic tradition (Mula Jadi Na Bolon; Batara Guru's raft; Naga Padoha), as recorded in van der Tuuk's Batak studies

summary.en: In the beginning was Mula Jadi Na Bolon, 'the origin of becoming,' alone in the void; he creates the three levels of the world and three sons to rule them. The middle world is spread as dry land over the primeval waters — supported, the Toba Batak say, on the raft Batara Guru made at the creation, and held upon the back of the underworld serpent Naga Padoha, whose stirrings are the earthquakes.
summary.zh: 太初有『形成之源』穆拉·賈迪·納·波隆，獨存於虛空；他造世界三層，並生三子以分掌之。中界乃鋪於原水之上之乾土——多巴巴塔克人說：大地枕於巴塔拉·古魯創世時所造之筏上，臥於地下巨蛇那伽·帕多哈之背；蛇之一動，即為地震。

sensitivity.note: Batak cosmogony; the raft detail is cited by Skeat (1900) from the J.R.A.S. Batak material; paraphrase of the standard telling.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the standard Batak cosmogonic account (van der Tuuk tradition); paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Batak cosmogony recorded in the great Batak studies of the nineteenth century tells how the world rests on agreements made in the deep past — and on a serpent who never agreed to them.

BEGINNING: THE ALONE ONE. Before everything was Mula Jadi Na Bolon, 'the origin of becoming,' alone in space, without companion or material. From his own substance he brings forth the framework of the cosmos in three levels — the upper world of the gods, the middle world of men, and the underworld of the dead and the powers below — and then three sons, to whom he allots these levels: Batara Guru in the highest, Sori Deak in the middle, and Mangalabulan below.

MIDDLE: THE RAFT AND THE SERPENT. The middle world is made habitable by spreading dry earth over the primeval waters; the earth rests, in the standard telling, on a raft which Batara Guru made for its support at the creation (the detail Skeat quotes from the J.R.A.S. Batak material). Beneath everything lies Naga Padoha, the great serpent of the underworld, on whose back the world-raft rides; when the serpent stirs — cramped, offended, or simply tired — the earth shakes, and the Batak offerings must remind him of his charge.

END: THE GRANDDAUGHTER'S DESCENT. To people the middle world, the line of the high god descends: Batara Guru's daughter (in the standard account the granddaughter of Mula Jadi Na Bolon) is sent down to the middle world and becomes the ancestress of mankind there; her descendants people the Toba highlands around the great lake, and the first of them, Si Raja Batak, is born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit. The three-level cosmos thus becomes a genealogy: the Batak live between the gods above and the serpent below, related to both.

FUNCTIONS. The cosmogony (1) explains the vertical order of the Batak universe and the places of ritual speech; (2) etiologizes earthquakes as the serpent's movement beneath the raft; (3) grounds the clans (marga) in a divine descent tied to Pusuk Buhit; and (4) supplies the world-serpent cluster's Sumatran highland form. The serpent's office is the cosmology's hinge: Naga Padoha is not a rebel to be defeated but a bearer to be maintained, and the Batak ritual address to him is contractual — offerings remind the serpent of the charge accepted at the creation, and earthquakes are read as arrears. The raft, likewise, is not merely a platform but a covenant-object: the world sits on something made, and made things can be renegotiated. To people the middle world, Batara Guru's daughter descends, and the genealogy that follows is the Batak system in miniature: the clans of the Toba country trace their marga to Si Raja Batak, born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit beside the lake, so that the cosmology's vertical levels — gods above, serpent below — are connected by a family tree running through the mountain's slopes. The story is told at both weddings and funerals, where the two directions of the vertical axis are invoked in turn.
narrative.zh: 十九世紀巴塔克研究記錄之創世論講述世界如何依遠古之約而安——以及一條從未應約之蛇。開篇：先有『形成之源』穆拉·賈迪·納·波隆，獨存無伴無材；自其本質生出三層宇宙（神之上界、人之中界、亡者與下方之力之下界），並生三子分掌：巴塔拉·古魯居最高，梭裏·迪亞克居中，芒加拉布蘭居下。中段：以乾土鋪於原水而使中界宜居；標準敘述云：地枕於巴塔拉·古魯創世時所造之筏（斯凱特引自J.R.A.S.巴塔克材料）；而萬物之下，臥著下界巨蛇那伽·帕多哈，世界之筏騎於其背；蛇一動（或拘、或怒、或倦），大地便震，巴塔克之祭品須提醒它記其職守。結尾：神裔降中界生民：巴塔拉·古魯之女（標準敘述中為穆拉之孫女）受遣下凡，成為人類之祖；其後裔繁於大湖周圍之多巴高地，其首者西·拉賈·巴塔克生於聖山普素·布希。三層宇宙於是成為譜系：巴塔克人上承諸神、下繫巨蛇，與兩界皆有血緣。功能：釋宇宙縱序與儀式語言之位、釋地震為筏下之蛇之動、以神裔繫氏族於聖山、並為世界蛇母題供給蘇門答臘高地之形態。

title.en: The Origin of Lake Toba: The Fisherman Who Broke the Taboo
title.zh: 多巴湖之由來：破禁的漁夫

region.en: Lake Toba and Samosir island, North Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘多巴湖與沙摩西島

texts.period: Toba Batak oral legend; recorded in 19th-20th century collections

source.archive: Indonesian oral tradition (Toba Batak legend cycle)
source.work: The legend of the origin of Lake Toba (Toba Batak oral tradition)

summary.en: The fisherman who casts his hook into the Toba valley catches a golden fish that becomes a woman; he marries her on one condition — that he never tell anyone she was once a fish. Years later, in anger at his son, he breaks the promise; that night the sky darkens, the rains fall without end, the valley sinks, and the wife returns to the water: the drowned valley is Lake Toba, and the island where she set down her son in the flood is Samosir.
summary.zh: 漁夫在多巴谷地垂釣，釣上一尾化為女子之金魚；他娶之，唯一條件：永不可對人言其曾為魚。多年後，他怒於其子而破誓；當夜天昏雨瀉不止，谷地下陷，妻子歸水——被淹之谷是多巴湖，而她在洪水中放下兒子之處，便是沙摩西島。

sensitivity.note: Best-known Toba Batak legend; taboo-broken-flood cluster.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the Toba Batak oral legend; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The origin legend of Lake Toba is the Toba Batak's great taboo-broken catastrophe story, told to explain the largest volcanic lake on earth and the island in its middle.

BEGINNING: THE GOLDEN FISH. A fisherman works the small rivers of the Toba valley and one day hooks a fish of golden shine; it speaks, and becomes a woman of great beauty. He marries her on her one condition: that he never tell anyone where she came from — that she was a fish of the water. They live well, and she bears a son.

MIDDLE: THE BROKEN SECRET. The boy grows hungry and greedy at meals, and one day the father, exhausted and furious, shouts the secret at him: 'You eat like the child of a fish — for your mother was a fish!' The word is out; the fish-wife hears it and grieves, for the promise that kept the world ordered is broken.

END: THE FLOODING OF THE VALLEY. That night the sky closes; rain falls without pause, and the waters rise from the earth as well as the sky. The wife returns to the water that made her, taking to safety the son she sets on the high ground that will become the island of Samosir; the father's valley floods entire. What had been fields and villages becomes Lake Toba, and the headland opposite Samosir keeps the father's name in the local tellings — the taboo's price still visible in the landscape.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) etiologizes Lake Toba and Samosir island; (2) polices the marriage-tell-no-origin taboo that governs many Batak affinity relationships; (3) supplies the Malay-world flood cluster with its highland Sumatran form; and (4) ties the landscape's topography to a moral memory told on every school trip to the lake. The legend's landscape is precise and checkable: Lake Toba fills a vast volcanic caldera, and Samosir is the island in its middle; the tellings align the boy's refuge with Samosir's high ground and keep the father's memory in the headland opposite. The moral architecture is equally exact: the fish-wife's single condition is the classic affinity taboo of the Batak world, in which a marriage partner's origin must not be named, and the father's breach is not mere anger but the public unmaking of the marriage's fiction — the word spoken aloud costs the world its surface. Village tellings distribute the blame variously: in some the son provokes the outburst, in others neighbours demand the secret, in others the father boasts; the flood follows the word, not the speaker. As comparative material, the legend belongs to the taboo-broken-flood cluster — Deucalion's flood, the sinking-village tales of Sundanese Situ Bagendit — with the distinctive feature that the survivor is the child of the taboo-breaker and the flood the return of the tabooed parent to her element.
narrative.zh: 多巴湖由來傳說乃多巴巴塔克最大之破禁災變故事，用以解釋世上最大火山湖及其中央之島。開篇：漁夫於多巴谷小河垂釣，一日釣得金光之魚；魚能言，化為美貌女子。他娶她，但只有一個條件：永不說出她的來歷——她本是水中之魚。二人生活美滿，得一子。中段：兒子進餐貪饞；一日父親疲憊憤怒，衝口而出：『你吃得像魚之子——因你母親本是魚！』誓言既破，魚妻聞言而悲——維持世界秩序的承諾已斷。結尾：當夜天閉，雨瀉不止，水自地中亦湧；妻子歸於其所從來之水，攜子置於高地——即日後之沙摩西島；父親的谷地盡沒。昔日田舍化為多巴湖，沙摩西對岸之岬在當地敘述中仍保留父親之名——禁忌之價，至今顯於山水。功能：釋多巴湖與沙摩西島、規訓巴塔克姻親之『勿言來歷』禁忌、為馬來世界洪水母題群供給蘇門答臘高地之形態、並將地貌與道德記憶繫於湖畔之講述。

title.en: Si Raja Batak: Born on the Holy Mountain
title.zh: 西·拉賈·巴塔克：生於聖山

region.en: Mount Pusuk Buhit, Toba Batak country, North Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘普素·布希山，多巴巴塔克之地

source.archive: Indonesian oral tradition (Toba Batak legend cycle)
source.work: The tradition of Si Raja Batak (Toba Batak ancestry)

summary.en: All the Toba Batak clans trace themselves to Si Raja Batak, the first man of the middle world, born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit beside Lake Toba. From his sons descend the great marga (clans) of the Batak country; the mountain remains the place where oaths are strongest and the oldest clan-songs return.
summary.zh: 多巴巴塔克諸氏族皆自『西·拉賈·巴塔克』——中界第一人——追溯血統；他生於多巴湖畔之聖山普素·布希。巴塔克大地之各大marga（氏族）皆其諸子之後；聖山至今為誓言最重之地，氏族最古之歌皆歸於此。

sensitivity.note: Clan-ancestry charter; careful with living clan claims, kept at tradition level.

passages.text: The Toba Batak clans trace their descent to Si Raja Batak, the first man of the middle world, born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit beside Lake Toba; from his sons descend the great marga of the Batak country. Pusuk Buhit remains the mountain of strongest oaths and the oldest clan-songs: genealogy, law and landscape are one in the Batak telling of the first man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Toba Batak ancestral tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: The Batak Ordeals: Rice That Turns to Stone
title.zh: 巴塔克神判：化為石頭的米

region.zh: 北蘇門答臘巴塔克之地

texts.period: Customs observed by Marsden 1784, History of Sumatra

source.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784), the oath-ordeals of the Batta people

summary.en: A person accused of a crime who asserts innocence may be acquitted by solemn oath, or by ordeal: a cock's throat is cut, and the accused, putting rice in his mouth, wishes it may turn to stone if he is guilty; or, holding up a musket bullet, wishes to be shot in that case. In weightier matters a small leaden or tin image is set in a dish of rice garnished with musket bullets, and the kneeling man prays that his crop may fail and his cattle die — and that he may never taste salt — if he lies.
summary.zh: 被控而自稱無辜者，可經莊嚴宣誓或神判而獲釋：割開公雞之喉，被告含米於口，祝曰若有罪則米化為石；或持火槍彈在手，祝曰若有罪則為彈所斃。重案則以鉛或錫小像置於撒有槍彈之米盤中，跪者禱曰：若吾說謊，願田禾絕收、牛群盡死、終身不得嘗鹽。

sensitivity.note: Eighteenth-century ethnography of Batak oath-law; the salt-curse remains a living idiom of oath-taking.

passages.text: A person accused of a crime who asserts innocence is in some cases acquitted by solemnly swearing to it, and is sometimes obliged to go through a kind of ordeal: a cock's throat is cut, the accused puts a little rice into his mouth and wishes it may become a stone if he is guilty of the crime charged.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784); not verbatim.

passages.text: In more important instances they put a small leaden or tin image into the middle of a dish of rice garnished with musket bullets, and the man, kneeling down, prays that his crop of paddy may fail, his cattle die, and that himself may never taste salt — which is regarded as necessary to existence — if he does not declare the truth.

title.en: The White Buffalo's Entrails: War Augury of the Batak

region.zh: 北蘇門答臘巴塔克之地

texts.period: Customs observed by Marsden 1784, History of Sumatra

source.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784), the war-divination of the Batta people

summary.en: Before going to war the Batak kill a perfectly white buffalo or fowl and judge the fortune of the campaign from the motion of the intestines. The priest who performs this ceremony 'had need to be infallible,' Marsden notes: if he predicts contrary to the event he is sometimes put to death for want of skill.
summary.zh: 出兵之前，巴塔克人宰殺純白之水牛或家禽，觀腸之動以判戰之吉凶。行此禮之祭司『必須無誤』——馬爾斯登記曰：若其預言與事實相反，有時即因『術之不精』而被處死。

sensitivity.note: Historical ethnography of sacrificial divination; noted as custom, not prescription.

passages.text: Before they go to war they kill a buffalo or a fowl that is perfectly white, and by observing the motion of the intestines they judge of the good or ill fortune that will attend them. The priest who performs this ceremony had need to be infallible, for if he predicts contrary to the event he is sometimes put to death for his want of skill — the augur's life staked with the army's fortune.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Marsden (1784); not verbatim.

title.en: The Months-Long Funeral: Dancing Round the Coffin, Fleeing the Fiend
title.zh: 經月之葬：繞棺之舞與逐鬼之奔

region.zh: 北蘇門答臘巴塔克之地

texts.period: Rites observed by Marsden 1784, History of Sumatra

source.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784), the funeral rites and ceremonies of the Batta people

summary.en: When a raja or person of consequence dies, the funeral may take up several months: the corpse is kept unburied in a hollowed gomuti-tree coffin sealed with dammar, a bamboo tube draining into the ground. When the relatives and creditors assemble, each woman brings a biscuit of rice and dances round the coffin; the priest, in robes cut like birds and beasts and painted various colours, swings buffalo flesh, kills a fowl over the body, then seizes a cocoanut-fibre broom and sweeps furiously about as if to chase away an evil spirit — at which four appointed men lift the coffin and run with it as if escaping the fiend, the priest sweeping after it for some distance before the grave is closed and buffalo horns nailed to the posts.
summary.zh: 拉賈或顯要亡故，葬禮常歷時數月：屍身不葬，置於鏤空之糖棕木棺，以達瑪脂封之，棺底插竹管入地排水。親友債主齊集之日，每位婦女攜米餅近屍，繞棺而舞歡飲；祭司身著鳥獸形彩衣，揮舞水牛肉、殺雞瀝血於棺，繼而抓起椰纖之帚狂掃四週如逐惡鬼——四名指定之人立時抬起棺木疾奔，如逃離魔掌，祭司追掃甚遠；墓既封，水牛之角釘於柱上，眾人乃安然散歸。

sensitivity.note: Historical ethnography of Batak funerary rite (as observed 1784); the modern rite differs — noted to avoid antiquarian fixity.

passages.text: When a raja or person of consequence dies, the funeral usually takes up several months: the corpse is kept unburied in a coffin of the hollowed gomuti tree well covered with dammar, a bamboo tube inserted below carrying away the matter into the ground till the bones alone remain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the people assemble each woman brings a biscuit of rice and places it near the corpse; they dance round it and make merry, killing buffaloes or horses for the feast. The priest, whose robes are cut into the shape of birds and beasts and painted of different colours, takes a piece of buffalo's flesh, swings it about in violent attitudes, and eats it voraciously; he kills a fowl over the dead body, letting the blood run upon the coffin.

He then takes a broom of cocoanut fibres and sweeps furiously about him as if to chase away some evil spirit; when suddenly four men appointed for the purpose lift up the coffin and run quickly off with it, as if escaping from the fiend, the priest continuing to sweep after it for some distance. It is then buried; the horns of the buffalos killed on the occasion are nailed to the posts, and the people depart in peace.

title.en: The Skull at the Raja's Door: Marsden's Testimony on the Old Feast
title.zh: 王邸門前之顱：馬爾斯登之證言

region.zh: 北蘇門答臘巴塔克之地（十八世紀）

texts.period: Recorded by Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784), from the accounts of residents and travellers

source.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784), the Batta customs section (skull trophy and feast accounts)

summary.en: Marsden records, from the converging testimony of English residents at Natal and Tappanooly, the old Batak custom of the prisoner's feast: Charles Miller's journal notes a man's skull hanging in the raja's hall 'placed there as a trophy, it being the skull of an enemy they had taken prisoner, whose body, according to the custom of the Battas, they had eaten about two months before' — a rite of absorbing the enemy's strength, Marsden argues, attested by old writers and recent witnesses alike.
summary.zh: 馬爾斯登據納塔爾與塔帕努利英國居民之一致證言，記錄巴塔克俘虜之宴古俗：查爾斯·米勒日記見拉賈廳中懸一人顱——『作為戰利品懸於此；此乃所擒之敵之顱，依巴塔克之俗，其身於約兩月前已食』——馬爾斯登論曰：此乃吸收敵力之儀，古書近證皆相合。

sensitivity.note: Historical ethnography of a discontinued rite; presented as eighteenth-century testimony, framed within its colonial context of reporting. No present-day community is accused.

passages.text: Charles Miller, in the journal quoted by Marsden, writes: 'In the house where the raja receives strangers we saw a man's skull hanging up, which the raja told us was placed there as a trophy, it being the skull of an enemy they had taken prisoner, whose body, according to the custom of the Battas, they had eaten about two months before.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the testimony quoted in Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784); not verbatim.

passages.text: Marsden gathers the converging accounts of the residents of Natal and Tappanooly and concludes that the experience of later days agrees with the uniform testimony of old writers — presenting the practice as a rite of the period, framed within the colonial context of its reporting.
